t.4.24.1: Seeing Vālin lifeless, Rāghava, the tormentor of foes, immediately thereafter spoke courteous words to Sugrīva.
t.4.24.2: The dead one is not joined to any good through the torment of grief. You should now attend to whatever must be done next in this matter.
t.4.24.3: The custom of the world must be followed; you have done your shedding of tears. No rite can be performed once its proper time has passed.
t.4.24.4: Destiny is the cause in this world; destiny is the means by which deeds are accomplished; destiny here is the cause that drives all beings to their appointed tasks.
t.4.24.5: No one is the doer of anything, nor is anyone master in the directing of it; the world moves according to its own nature, and Time is its final resort.
t.4.24.6: Time does not pass beyond time, nor does time ever fall short; and having attained his own nature, no one ever goes beyond it.
t.4.24.7: Time knows no kinship, no reason, no valor; no tie of friend or kinsman is a cause that moves it, nor is it subject even to its own will.
t.4.24.8: But one who sees rightly must take into account the turning of time; righteousness, wealth, and pleasure are all ordered by the course of time.
t.4.24.10: Through his union with his own dharma, that great-souled one, not guarding his life, has won heaven and taken possession of it.
t.4.24.9: From here Vālin has gone to his own true state, O lord of the monkeys; he has obtained the fruit of his deeds, made pure through the union of dharma, artha and kāma.
t.4.24.12: But at the end of Rāma's words, Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, spoke courteous words to Sugrīva, who had lost his senses.
t.4.24.11: This indeed is the supreme destiny which the leader of the monkey troops has attained. Therefore enough of grieving; let what the time now calls for be attended to.
t.4.24.13: O Sugrīva, together with Tārā and Aṅgada, perform his funeral rites without delay and see to the cremation of Vālin.
t.4.24.14: Give orders for logs of wood, dry and plentiful, and for celestial sandalwood, for the sake of Vālin's funeral rites.
t.4.24.15: Console this Aṅgada, whose heart is downcast. Do not be foolish-minded; this city now depends on you.
t.4.24.16: Let Aṅgada bring garlands and garments of various kinds, ghee and oil, and perfumes too, and whatever else is needed here next.
t.4.24.17: You, Tāra, quickly fetch a palanquin and come in haste, for speed is beneficial and fitting, especially at a time like this.
t.4.24.18: Let the monkeys who are accustomed to bearing palanquins make themselves ready; strong and capable, they will carry Vālin away.
t.4.24.19: Having spoken thus to Sugrīva, Lakṣmaṇa, who increased the joy of Sumitrā and slew hostile heroes, stood there, remaining near his brother.
t.4.24.20: Hearing Lakṣmaṇa's words, Tāra, his mind agitated, swiftly entered the cave, his thoughts fixed upon the palanquin.
t.4.24.21: Tāra, having fetched the palanquin, came back again, the litter being borne by valiant vānaras well suited to carrying it.
t.4.24.22: Then Sugrīva, lifting up Vālin, placed him on the litter, wailing loudly, together with Aṅgada.
t.4.24.23: Having placed upon the palanquin the lifeless Vālin, adorned with various ornaments, garlands and garments,
t.4.24.24: Then King Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, gave the command: "Let the funeral rites of my noble elder brother be performed in a fitting manner."
t.4.24.25: Let the monkeys go in front, distributing many jewels of various kinds, and let the palanquin follow immediately after them.
t.4.24.26: They swiftly performed the funeral rites for Vālin with all the special splendour that is seen for kings upon the earth.
t.4.24.27: Quickly taking hold of Aṅgada, all the monkeys led by Tāra, whose kinsman had been slain, set out wailing.
t.4.24.28: All the female monkeys, led by Tārā, whose lord of the troop had been slain, followed their husband, wailing with piteous cries.
t.4.24.29: With the sound of the weeping of those she-monkeys in the depths of the forest, all the woods and mountains seemed to cry out on every side.
t.4.24.30: On a secluded sandbank of a mountain river, surrounded by water, a great many forest-roaming monkeys built a funeral pyre.
t.4.24.31: Then the bearers, accustomed to carrying, lowered the palanquin from their shoulders, and all of them, overcome with grief, withdrew to a secluded spot and stood there.
t.4.24.32: Then Tārā, seeing her husband lying upon the floor of the litter, placed his head in her lap and, deeply grief-stricken, lamented.
t.4.24.33: And why do you gaze upon these people stricken with grief? O giver of honour, though your life has departed, your face seems joyful, and it appears with the hue of the setting sun, as if it were the face of one still living.
t.4.24.34: It is Time, in the form of Rāma, that drags you away, O monkey, Time by whom all of us have been made widows with a single arrow in battle.
t.4.24.35: O lord of kings, here are those she-monkeys who were always dear to you; they have come on foot over a long road. Why do you not awaken?
t.4.24.36: Surely these moon-faced wives were dear to you; why then do you not look upon them now, nor upon Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys?
t.4.24.37: Indeed, O king, these ministers of yours, headed by Tāra, and these people dwelling in the city are sitting all around you, O sinless one.
t.4.24.39: Then the female monkeys, themselves wasted with grief, raised up Tārā, who was lamenting thus, overwhelmed by sorrow for her husband.
t.4.24.38: Dismiss these mighty ones as is fitting, O subduer of foes; then all of us, flushed with wine, shall sport together in the forests.
t.4.24.40: Then Aṅgada, weeping, his senses stricken by grief, placed his father upon the funeral pyre together with Sugrīva.
t.4.24.42: Having cremated Vālin according to the prescribed rites, those monkeys then came to the auspicious river of cool waters to offer the water oblations.
t.4.24.41: Then, having duly applied the fire, he, his senses distraught, walked around his father, who had set out on the long journey, keeping him on his left.
t.4.24.43: Then, all together there, placing Aṅgada in front, they, accompanied by Sugrīva and Tārā, poured out water for Vālin.
t.4.24.44: Becoming dejected together with the dejected Sugrīva, the mighty Kākutstha, sharing the same grief, had the funeral rites performed.
